title: Tariffs can reach domestic prices indirectly and with a long delay
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35561; 2025 U.S. tariffs, consumer prices, imported inputs, domestic markups, and less-exposed comparison goods
geography: United States; consumer goods and domestic producers exposed to the 2025 tariff changes

consumer_pass_through.value: about 26% of the tariff increase passed through to consumer prices relative to less-exposed goods

direct_share.value: 64% of the consumer-price increase was direct through higher prices of foreign varieties

indirect_share.value: 36% arose through imported-input costs and higher domestic markups as imports became less competitive

timing.value: the indirect effect took approximately nine to twelve months to work through supply chains
timing.unit: lag from tariff change to indirect consumer-price effect

observations.method: The authors study 2025 U.S. tariffs, compare exposed goods with less-exposed goods while holding aggregate conditions fixed, and decompose consumer-price effects into direct import-price and indirect input-cost and domestic-markup channels.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not identify each household's full basket, wages, debt, quantity, package size, quality, store choice, or political response. The estimate is relative to less-exposed goods and depends on the study's exposure and timing design; the nine-to-twelve-month lag is an aggregate supply-chain pattern, not a universal household schedule.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumer goods and domestic producers with different import exposure, imported-input dependence, competition, inventory, and supplier relationships; household burden can differ by product basket and ability to substitute.
observations.counterinterpretation: Firms may absorb some costs, change suppliers, reduce package size or quality, or use existing inventory before raising prices. A domestic markup increase can reflect changed competitive conditions rather than a direct tariff charge, and a later price increase can also reflect unrelated shocks. A higher price does not by itself establish the household's welfare loss or policy judgment.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35561

boundary: This record adds a tariff-to-price pathway with separate direct and delayed indirect channels. It does not establish a particular household's total cost, quantity or quality loss, wage or job effect, political blame, or whether any later domestic production benefit offsets the consumer burden.
